items.title: United States: Trump's second term heads into the midterms
items.actors:
- **President**: Donald Trump (Republican), in his second term since January 2025
- **Vice President**: J.D. Vance, who also casts tie-breaking votes in the Senate
- **Speaker of the House**: Mike Johnson (R), managing one of the narrowest House majorities in modern times
- **House Minority Leader**: Hakeem Jeffries (D), favoured to become Speaker if Democrats flip the House
- **Senate Majority Leader**: John Thune (R), leading a 53–47 Republican Senate
- **Senate Minority Leader**: Chuck Schumer (D)
- **Federal Reserve Chair**: Kevin Warsh, sworn in on 22 May 2026 as the Fed's 17th chair, succeeding Jerome Powell
items.timeline:
- **1776**: Declaration of Independence; the Constitution follows in 1787
- **1861–1865**: Civil War ends slavery and reshapes federal power
- **1945**: US emerges from World War II as a superpower and builds the postwar order (UN, NATO in 1949, Bretton Woods)
- **1991**: Collapse of the Soviet Union leaves the US as sole superpower
- **2001**: 9/11 attacks lead to wars in Afghanistan and Iraq
- **2008**: Global financial crisis; Barack Obama elected
- **2017–2021**: Trump's first term; 2020 election won by Joe Biden
- **2024**: Trump defeats Kamala Harris; Republicans win both chambers
- **2025**: Sweeping tariff programme under emergency powers; long autumn government shutdown
- **2026**: Supreme Court strikes down emergency-power tariffs; Warsh takes over the Fed; midterms set for 3 November
items.issues:
- **Midterm control of Congress**: Democrats need a net gain of a handful of House seats and four Senate seats to take control
- **Tariffs and trade**: after the Supreme Court curbed emergency-power tariffs, trade deals with partners are being reworked
- **Monetary policy**: the Warsh-led Fed has held rates at 3.50–3.75% and signalled that a hike is not ruled out while inflation stays sticky
- **Presidential approval**: Trump's net approval sits at a term low in several trackers
- **Budget fights and shutdown risk**: recurring standoffs over federal funding and the scope of executive power
- **Foreign commitments**: Ukraine, NATO burden-sharing, and troop posture in Europe and Asia
items.current: With the 3 November midterms days away, Republicans hold the Senate 53–47 and a razor-thin House majority under Speaker Mike Johnson. Forecasters and prediction markets lean towards a Democratic House: as of mid-October Cook rated 214 seats as at least leaning Democratic, Democrats led most generic-ballot averages by roughly 5–11 points, and [Kalshi traders put Democratic odds of taking the House near 90% and the Senate around 63%](https://news.kalshi.com/p/2026-midterm-predictions). Senate battlegrounds include Maine, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas and Texas. President Trump's approval is at a low point in several trackers, and Johnson is [campaigning to defend the majority](https://www.ajc.com/news/2026/10/house-speaker-mike-johnson-draws-on-faith-as-he-fights-to-hold-the-republican-majority/) in swing districts. On the economy, Kevin Warsh, [sworn in as Fed chair on 22 May](https://www.mpamag.com/us/mortgage-industry/industry-trends/key-dates-that-will-define-kevin-warshs-opening-months-as-fed-chair/576298), has kept the policy rate at 3.50–3.75% and named the October and December meetings as key decision points. A Democratic House would give the opposition subpoena power and leverage over spending for the final two years of Trump's term.

items.title: Poland: cohabitation between a nationalist president and a pro-EU government
items.actors:
- **President**: Karol Nawrocki, PiS-backed, in office since August 2025; a record user of the veto
- **Prime Minister**: Donald Tusk, Civic Coalition (KO), formally KO leader since March 2026
- **Governing coalition**: KO, Polish People's Party (PSL), Poland 2050, New Left, plus the Centre group that split from Poland 2050
- **Sejm Speaker**: Włodzimierz Czarzasty (New Left)
- **Foreign Minister**: Radosław Sikorski (KO), also deputy PM
- **Defence Minister**: Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (PSL), also deputy PM
- **Justice Minister**: Waldemar Żurek, leading the rule-of-law reversal
- **Main opposition**: Law and Justice (PiS) under Jarosław Kaczyński, with Przemysław Czarnek as PM candidate; far-right Confederation parties are rising
items.timeline:
- **1918**: Poland regains independence after 123 years of partition
- **1939–1945**: Invaded by Germany and the USSR; huge wartime losses including the Holocaust
- **1980**: Solidarity trade union founded in Gdańsk
- **1989**: Round Table talks and semi-free elections end communist rule
- **1999**: Joins NATO
- **2004**: Joins the European Union
- **2015**: PiS wins power and begins judicial overhaul that triggers EU rule-of-law disputes
- **2023**: Tusk-led coalition wins the October election and takes office in December
- **2025**: Nawrocki narrowly wins the presidency; Tusk survives a confidence vote
- **2026**: Nawrocki vetoes the KRS judicial reform (February); KO loses the Kraków mayoralty after a recall (May–October)
items.issues:
- **Rule of law and the judiciary**: the coalition cannot unwind PiS-era judicial changes, including the KRS judicial council, while the president vetoes reforms
- **Presidential vetoes**: Nawrocki vetoed 41 laws in his first year, blocking tax measures worth an estimated PLN 7–8 billion; the coalition lacks the 60% needed to override
- **2027 election**: a parliamentary vote is due by 11 November 2027, with KO ahead of PiS but the far right gaining
- **Security**: defence spending among NATO's highest, plus a push for a permanent US base
- **Coalition cohesion**: Poland 2050's split and debates over a joint list strain the government
- **Ukraine**: support for Kyiv balanced against farm-trade and refugee-benefit tensions
items.current: Poland remains locked in cohabitation. President Karol Nawrocki, now past his first year in office, has vetoed more laws than any president since 1989: [41 vetoes in year one, blocking revenue measures worth up to PLN 7.3 billion](https://polskieradio.pl/395/7784/Artykul/3716939,vetoes-by-polands-nawrocki-may-have-cost-budget-up-to-pln-73-billion-portal-says). In February he also [vetoed the government's bill to restore the judicial council's independence](https://www.freemalaysiatoday.com/category/world/2026/02/20/polands-president-vetoes-bill-restoring-courts-independence), and Donald Tusk's coalition lacks the three-fifths majority needed to override him. The government (KO, PSL, Poland 2050, New Left and the breakaway Centre group) is looking ahead to parliamentary elections due by November 2027. PiS has named Przemysław Czarnek as its PM candidate, while far-right Confederation parties gain ground. In October KO suffered a symbolic defeat when independent Łukasz Gibała won Kraków's mayoralty. Abroad, Nawrocki has pressed Washington for a permanent US base, and Tusk made an official visit to India on 21–23 October.

items.title: Kraków: a recall, a new independent mayor, and fights over clean air and transport
items.actors:
- **Mayor (Prezydent Miasta)**: Łukasz Gibała, independent, won the 11 October 2026 run-off with about 62% and was sworn in around 20 October
- **Former mayor**: Aleksander Miszalski (KO), removed in the 24 May 2026 recall referendum two years into his term
- **Acting commissioner (May–October 2026)**: Stanisław Kracik, appointed by PM Tusk to run the city until the new mayor took office
- **Defeated run-off candidate**: Senator Monika Piątkowska, joint KO–PSL candidate
- **City Council (Rada Miasta Krakowa)**: 43 councillors elected in 2024; a parallel referendum to dissolve it failed on turnout
- **Małopolska Voivode (central government)**: Krzysztof Klęczar (PSL), in office since December 2023
- **Marshal of Małopolska (regional self-government)**: Łukasz Smółka (PiS), elected July 2024 after a long deadlock in the regional assembly
items.timeline:
- **1038**: Becomes capital of Poland, a role it holds until the court moves to Warsaw around 1596
- **1364**: Jagiellonian University founded, one of Europe's oldest
- **1978**: Historic centre among the first sites on UNESCO's World Heritage List; Archbishop Karol Wojtyła becomes Pope John Paul II
- **1990**: First democratic local government after the fall of communism
- **2002–2024**: Jacek Majchrowski serves as mayor for over two decades
- **2019**: Małopolska's household solid-fuel ban makes Kraków the first Polish city to ban coal and wood heating
- **2024**: Miszalski narrowly beats Gibała (about 51%) to become mayor
- **2026**: Revised Clean Transport Zone takes effect (1 July); Miszalski recalled (May); Gibała elected (October)
items.issues:
- **Clean Transport Zone (SCT)**: the low-emission zone fuelled the recall; Gibała has promised a referendum on its future
- **Metro/premetro**: the city's flagship underground plan faces doubts about cost and timing; the acting commissioner put a realistic start at 2040–2045
- **Public transport and trams**: fare rises were a major grievance; tram extensions and service quality remain priorities
- **City finances**: high debt and a strained budget, with the new mayor pledging to end cronyism in appointments
- **Housing and overtourism**: pressure from short-term rentals and development; Gibała favours residents over developers and limits on short-term lets
- **Air quality**: smog has improved since the heating ban, but traffic emissions remain a concern
items.current: Kraków has a new mayor after an unusual year. On 24 May residents voted overwhelmingly to recall KO mayor Aleksander Miszalski, [with turnout just clearing the validity threshold](https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/05/25/mayor-of-krakow-dismissed-in-rare-recall-referendum/), while a parallel bid to dissolve the city council fell short. Commissioner Stanisław Kracik ran the city in the interim. In the early election, [independent Łukasz Gibała beat KO–PSL candidate Monika Piątkowska by about 62% to 38%](https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/11/independent-beats-pm-tusks-candidate-in-krakow-mayoral-election/) on 11 October, a blow to PM Tusk a year before national elections. Gibała, a former Civic Platform MP, now needs to work with a council elected in 2024. His pledges include a referendum on the Clean Transport Zone, which was revised from 1 July, fixing the city's finances, reversing ticket-price rises, and curbing short-term rentals. The [long-promised metro now looks distant](https://bezprawnik.pl/nowy-prezydent-krakowa-odziedziczy-bombe/), with a realistic start put at 2040–2045.

items.title: India: Modi's coalition era, a resurgent BJP in the states, and youth unrest
items.actors:
- **Prime Minister**: Narendra Modi (BJP), in a third term since 2024 that relies on NDA allies such as the TDP and JD(U)
- **Home Minister**: Amit Shah (BJP)
- **External Affairs Minister**: S. Jaishankar
- **Defence Minister**: Rajnath Singh
- **Finance Minister**: Nirmala Sitharaman; Piyush Goyal holds Commerce and is leading the trade talks with the US
- **Education Minister**: Pralhad Joshi, who replaced Dharmendra Pradhan after he resigned over the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak
- **Leader of the Opposition (Lok Sabha)**: Rahul Gandhi (Congress)
- **New state leaders (2026)**: Suvendu Adhikari (BJP, West Bengal), Vijay (TVK, Tamil Nadu), V.D. Satheesan (Congress/UDF, Kerala)
items.timeline:
- **1947**: Independence and Partition; Jawaharlal Nehru becomes PM
- **1950**: Constitution adopted; India becomes a republic
- **1975–1977**: Indira Gandhi's Emergency suspends civil liberties
- **1991**: Balance-of-payments crisis triggers economic liberalisation
- **1998**: Nuclear tests at Pokhran
- **2014**: Modi leads the BJP to its first outright Lok Sabha majority
- **2019**: BJP re-elected; Article 370 revoked in Jammu and Kashmir
- **2024**: BJP loses its majority but Modi forms an NDA coalition government; Rahul Gandhi becomes Leader of the Opposition
- **2026**: BJP wins West Bengal for the first time; TVK takes Tamil Nadu and the UDF wins Kerala (results 4 May); education minister resigns over exam leak
items.issues:
- **Electoral roll revision**: the opposition says mass deletions from voter lists are politically motivated; the Election Commission denies it
- **Youth discontent**: exam paper leaks and jobs have sparked Gen Z-led protests
- **US trade deal and tariffs**: a deal to settle 2025's punitive US tariffs is nearly done
- **Federalism and the states**: centre–state friction, especially with opposition-run southern states
- **China and Pakistan**: border management with China and tensions with Pakistan
- **Next electoral tests**: 2027 state polls, including Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Gujarat, ahead of the 2029 general election
items.current: Narendra Modi governs in his third term at the head of the NDA coalition. The BJP was strengthened by the May 2026 state results: it [won West Bengal for the first time](https://worldview.ranenetwork.com/content/analysis/2026-05-11/in-india-the-bjp-s-state-election-wins-set-the-stage-for-national-reform), where Suvendu Adhikari is now chief minister, and the NDA held Assam and Puducherry. Elsewhere the picture was mixed: actor Vijay's TVK took Tamil Nadu and the Congress-led UDF won Kerala. The government has since been shaken by the NEET-UG paper leak. Youth protests forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign, and [Pralhad Joshi was named his replacement](https://english.aaj.tv/news/330465130). Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi is trying to turn Gen Z anger and disputes over the voter-roll revision into a unified challenge, while Home Minister Amit Shah predicts another Congress defeat in 2029. Abroad, New Delhi is close to a trade deal with Washington and hosted Polish PM Donald Tusk in October.

items.title: US–Poland: close military allies with prickly politics
items.actors:
- **US President**: Donald Trump, who has a warm rapport with President Nawrocki
- **Polish President**: Karol Nawrocki, champion of a permanent US base dubbed "Fort Trump"
- **Polish PM**: Donald Tusk, whose government handles most defence planning but has a cooler relationship with the White House
- **US Ambassador to Poland**: Thomas (Tom) Rose, confirmed in 2025
- **Polish Head of Mission in Washington**: Bogdan Klich, leading the embassy without full ambassadorial status amid a president–government dispute over appointments
- **Polish Deputy Defence Minister**: Stanisław Wziątek, a key voice on base planning
- **Sejm Speaker**: Włodzimierz Czarzasty, with whom the US ambassador cut contact in February 2026
items.timeline:
- **1919**: US recognises the reborn Polish state; Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points had backed Polish independence
- **1989**: US supports Poland's democratic transition and economic reforms
- **1999**: Poland joins NATO with strong US backing
- **2003**: Polish troops join the US-led invasion of Iraq
- **2016**: NATO enhanced Forward Presence brings rotational US forces to Poland
- **2020**: Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement signed
- **2022**: Poland becomes the main hub for Western aid to Ukraine; US–Poland nuclear power deal chooses Westinghouse
- **2023–2024**: Camp Kościuszko permanent garrison in Poznań (2023) and the Aegis Ashore missile-defence site at Redzikowo (2024) become operational
- **2026**: US envoy cuts ties with the Sejm Speaker (February); Washington cancels a deployment of about 4,000 troops (May); Poland requests a permanent base (June)
items.issues:
- **Permanent US base ("Fort Trump")**: location, troop numbers (3,000–5,000 planned) and a Polish cost estimate above PLN 15 billion
- **US troop levels**: rotational forces fell to about 6,500–7,000 after the May cancellation; Warsaw hopes for about 15,000
- **Arms purchases**: Poland buys heavily from the US, including Patriot, HIMARS, Abrams, Apache and F-35, which made up about 44% of its 2021–2025 arms imports
- **Political friction**: Trump's ties to the PiS camp versus tensions with Tusk's coalition; the Czarzasty episode
- **Ukraine and Russia**: differing emphases on how to end the war and the security guarantees to follow
items.current: Military ties are deepening even as political relations stay uneven. After talks with Donald Trump, President Karol Nawrocki said in September that a [permanent US base is "confirmed" and could be named Fort Trump](https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/09/23/new-us-fort-trump-military-base-in-poland-confirmed-says-president-nawrocki/). Planners talk of about 4,500 troops, with Poznań among the candidate sites, though no formal agreement or location has been announced and an announcement before the US midterms is possible. The push follows Washington's May cancellation of a roughly 4,000-strong deployment, which cut the rotational presence to about 6,500–7,000. Relations with Tusk's government are cooler. In February, US Ambassador Tom Rose [cut off contact with Sejm Speaker Włodzimierz Czarzasty](https://euronews.com/2026/02/06/us-cuts-diplomatic-ties-with-polish-sejm-speaker-wlodzimierz-czarzasty) over remarks critical of Trump. Poland's embassy in Washington is led by Bogdan Klich as head of mission because the president and government are deadlocked over ambassadorial appointments.

items.title: US–India: rebuilding after the 2025 tariff rupture
items.actors:
- **US President**: Donald Trump
- **Indian PM**: Narendra Modi
- **US Ambassador to India**: Sergio Gor, a close Trump aide who is also special envoy for South and Central Asia
- **Indian Ambassador to the US**: Vinay Mohan Kwatra, in post since August 2024
- **Indian Commerce Minister**: Piyush Goyal, leading the trade negotiations
- **External Affairs Minister**: S. Jaishankar
- **US Vice President**: J.D. Vance, who visited India in 2025
items.timeline:
- **1971**: US tilts toward Pakistan in the Bangladesh war; India signs a friendship treaty with the USSR
- **1998**: US sanctions follow India's nuclear tests
- **2000**: Bill Clinton's visit begins a thaw
- **2005–2008**: Civil nuclear agreement ends India's nuclear isolation
- **2016**: US designates India a Major Defense Partner
- **2017**: Quad (US, India, Japan, Australia) revived
- **2023**: Modi state visit; iCET technology initiative and jet-engine co-production deal
- **2025**: Trade talks open, then punitive US tariffs (linked in part to Russian oil purchases) strain ties
- **2026**: US Supreme Court strikes down emergency-power tariffs, forcing a rework of the deal text; envoys say an agreement is "very close"
items.issues:
- **Bilateral trade agreement**: a first tranche is in legal drafting; the goal is $500 billion in trade within three years, up from over $250 billion
- **Tariffs and market access**: India wants better terms than its competitors after the 2025 punitive duties
- **Russian oil**: a Senate-passed bill threatening 100% tariffs on buyers of Russian oil hangs over India
- **Defence and technology**: co-production, critical minerals, semiconductors and the Quad agenda
- **Immigration and visas**: H-1B rules and deportations affect Indian workers and students
items.current: Washington and New Delhi are close to completing a trade agreement meant to close out a turbulent 2025, when punitive US tariffs pushed ties to their lowest point in years. On 15 October US Ambassador Sergio Gor said the sides are ["very close" and the deal will be a "win-win"](https://www.businesstoday.in/india/story/we-are-very-close-us-envoy-sergio-gor-says-india-us-trade-deal-will-happen-561920-2026-10-15). Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said the first tranche is in legal drafting. The text had to be [reconfigured after the US Supreme Court struck down tariffs imposed under emergency powers](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/economy-and-policy/india-us-trade-deal-almost-done-ambassador-sergio-gor-text-being-finalised). Most substantive issues are reportedly settled. Trump and Modi have set a target of $500 billion in two-way trade within three years. Remaining irritants include a Senate-backed bill threatening steep tariffs on buyers of Russian oil and US immigration and visa policy. India is represented in Washington by Ambassador Vinay Mohan Kwatra.

items.title: Poland–India: a young strategic partnership gathers pace
items.actors:
- **Polish PM**: Donald Tusk, who made an official visit to India on 21–23 October 2026
- **Indian PM**: Narendra Modi, who in 2024 made the first visit to Poland by an Indian PM in 45 years
- **Polish Foreign Minister**: Radosław Sikorski, who visited New Delhi in January 2026
- **Indian External Affairs Minister**: S. Jaishankar, who visited Poland in September 2026
- **Polish President**: Karol Nawrocki
- **EU framework**: the India–EU free trade agreement concluded in January 2026 sets the wider frame for trade
items.timeline:
- **1942–1948**: The Maharaja Jam Sahib of Nawanagar shelters about 1,000 Polish refugee children, the 'Good Maharaja' story still central to ties
- **1954**: Diplomatic relations established; Indian embassy in Warsaw opens in 1957
- **1979**: PM Morarji Desai visits Poland, the last Indian PM visit until 2024
- **2004**: Poland joins the EU and becomes India's leading economic partner in Central Europe
- **2010**: Tusk makes his first visit to India as PM
- **2024**: Modi visits Warsaw; relations raised to a Strategic Partnership with an Action Plan for 2024–2028; social security agreement signed
- **2025**: Bilateral trade reaches about $6.4 billion, up 192% since 2013
- **2026**: India–EU FTA concluded (January); Sikorski and Jaishankar exchange visits; Tusk visits New Delhi and Bengaluru (October)
items.issues:
- **Trade growth and balance**: Poland wants to raise trade from about $6.5 billion to $10 billion; the balance strongly favours India
- **Defence industry**: Poland wants to sell military equipment and co-produce with India
- **Technology and research**: links in AI, cybersecurity, digital payments and between Poland's Łukasiewicz network and India's CSIR and IITs
- **Russia and Ukraine**: Warsaw's hard line on Moscow contrasts with India's ties to Russia
- **People-to-people**: students, the Jamsaheb youth exchange, and Indian workers in Poland
items.current: Relations are at their most active in decades. Donald Tusk [began a three-day visit to India on 21 October](https://ddindia.co.in/2026/10/poland-pm-begins-three-day-india-visit-to-hold-talks-with-pm-modi-on-thursday/), his first as PM since 2010. He held talks with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and with Narendra Modi at Hyderabad House on 22 October, then took a business delegation to Bengaluru. The agenda covered trade and investment, defence, emerging technologies, renewable energy and education. Ahead of the visit, [Poland signalled](https://www.outlookindia.com/international/donald-tusk-india-visit-october-21-defence-trade-space) that it hopes to lift trade from about $6.5 billion to $10 billion and expand defence exports and research links. The visit builds on the Strategic Partnership agreed during Modi's 2024 trip to Warsaw, on foreign-minister visits in both directions this year, and on the India–EU free trade agreement concluded in January, which should ease market access. According to [India's foreign ministry](https://www.mea.gov.in/Portal/ForeignRelation/India-Poland-Relations-010726.pdf), trade reached $6.36 billion in 2025.
